changes.before: and said, “Let Us make humankind in Our image and likeness, and let them rule the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the animals, the whole earth, and every creeping creature that moves upon the earth.”
changes.after: and said, “Let Us make man in Our image and likeness, and let him rule the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the animals, the whole earth, and every creeping creature that moves upon the earth.”
changes.reason: The Latin has singular hominem and singular praesit (“let him rule”), and the 9 November pass already rendered the same hominem/illum as “man … him” in 1:27, so the plural “humankind … them” misstates the Vulgate and clashes with the next verse.

changes.before: but concerning the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden, God commanded us not to eat it or touch it, lest we die.”
changes.after: but concerning the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden, God commanded us not to eat it or touch it, lest perhaps we die.”
changes.reason: The Vulgate has ne forte moriamur (“lest perhaps we die”), and that hesitant forte, set against God’s flat morte morieris in 2:17, is a well-known Vulgate reading that the column should keep.

changes.before: After his birth he lived eight hundred fifteen years and fathered sons and daughters.
changes.after: After Kenan’s birth he lived eight hundred fifteen years and fathered sons and daughters.
changes.reason: Post cujus ortum means “after whose birth,” referring to Kenan (Cainan), who was just named in 5:9; read aloud, “after his birth” sounds like Enosh’s own birth.

changes.before: He named him Noah, saying, “This one shall comfort us in our work and the toil of our hands upon the ground the Lord has cursed.”
changes.after: He named him Noah, saying, “This one shall comfort us from the work and toil of our hands upon the ground the Lord has cursed.”
changes.reason: Consolabitur nos ab operibus et laboribus manuum nostrarum means comfort or relief from the works and labours of our hands, with both nouns going with “of our hands”; “in our work” loses the sense of relief carried by ab.

changes.before: All flesh that moved upon the earth perished: birds, livestock, wild animals, and all creeping creatures that creep upon the earth, and all human beings.
changes.after: All flesh that moved upon the earth perished: birds, animals, wild beasts, and all creeping creatures that creep upon the earth, and all human beings.
changes.reason: The list is volucrum, animantium, bestiarum, so the second item is animantia (animals or living creatures) and not jumenta; “livestock” brings in a category that this verse’s Latin does not name.

changes.before: The Lord came down to see the city and tower that Adam's children were building.
changes.after: The Lord came down to see the city and tower that the children of Adam were building.
changes.reason: Latin filii Adam means Adam's descendants (humankind); “Adam's children” suggests his literal sons when heard aloud.

changes.before: Come, therefore, let Us go down and confuse their language there, so that each may not understand the speech of his neighbor.”
changes.after: Come, therefore, let Us go down and confuse their language there, so that none of them may understand the speech of his neighbor.”
changes.reason: ut non audiat unusquisque vocem proximi sui means no one is to understand his neighbour; “each may not understand” is ambiguous aloud (could mean “not everyone”).

changes.before: The people of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners before the Lord.
changes.after: The people of Sodom were very wicked, and exceedingly great sinners before the Lord.
changes.reason: Latin has two intensifiers, pessimi (very wicked) and peccatores … nimis (sinners exceedingly); the current reading merges them and drops the second.

changes.before: Abram said, “Lord God, what will You give me? I go on without children, and the son of my household's steward is this Eliezer of Damascus.”
changes.after: Abram said, “Lord God, what will You give me? I shall go without children, and the son of my household's steward is this Eliezer of Damascus.”
changes.reason: vadam is future (“I shall go”, i.e. I shall depart this life childless), not present “I go on”.

changes.before: Sarai said to Abram, “You deal unjustly with me. I gave my maidservant into your embrace, and when she saw that she had conceived, she held me in contempt. May the Lord judge between me and you.”
changes.after: Sarai said to Abram, “You deal unjustly with me. I gave my maidservant into your embrace, and now that she sees she has conceived, she holds me in contempt. May the Lord judge between me and you.”
changes.reason: videns quod conceperit, despectui me habet is present (seeing … she holds me in contempt): Sarai complains of ongoing contempt, not a past episode.

changes.before: Again he said, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, beyond numbering for their multitude.”
changes.after: Again he said, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, and they shall be too many to be counted.”
changes.reason: et non numerabitur præ multitudine = it shall not be counted for its great number; “beyond numbering for their multitude” is hard to follow aloud.

changes.before: A male whose foreskin's flesh has not been circumcised—that person shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken My covenant.”
changes.after: A male whose foreskin's flesh has not been circumcised—that person shall be blotted out from his people, because he has broken My covenant.”
changes.reason: delebitur is “shall be blotted out/destroyed” (the same verb rendered “destroy” for delebo in 18:28–32); “cut off” reflects the Hebrew karat, not the Latin. Builds on, does not revert, the 9 Nov edit.

changes.before: “Since I have begun,” he said, “I will speak to my Lord. What if twenty are found there?” He said, “I will not destroy them for the sake of the twenty.”
changes.after: “Since I have begun,” he said, “I will speak to my Lord. What if twenty are found there?” He said, “I will not kill them for the sake of the twenty.”
changes.reason: The Latin varies the verb in each reply (delebo, percutiam, faciam, interficiam, delebo); interficiam is “kill”, and rendering it “destroy” blurs it with delebo.

changes.before: Abraham named his son whom Sarah bore him Isaac,
changes.after: Abraham named his son, whom Sarah bore him, Isaac,
changes.reason: Latin sets the relative clause ‘quem genuit ei Sara’ inside the naming; commas keep listeners from hearing ‘bore him Isaac’ as one phrase.

changes.before: God said to him, “Do not let this seem harsh to you concerning the boy and your maidservant. Listen to Sarah in everything she tells you, for through Isaac your offspring shall be named.
changes.after: God said to him, “Do not let this seem harsh to you concerning the boy and your maidservant. In everything Sarah tells you, listen to her voice, for through Isaac your offspring shall be named.
changes.reason: Latin ‘audi vocem ejus’ keeps the ‘listen to her voice’ idiom that the column preserves elsewhere (27:13, 27:43); ‘listen to Sarah’ dropped it.

changes.before: When the water in the skin was exhausted, she laid the boy beneath one of the trees there.
changes.after: When the water in the skin was exhausted, she cast the boy down beneath one of the trees there.
changes.reason: Latin ‘abjecit puerum’ means she cast or threw the boy down (in despair), not that she gently ‘laid’ him.

changes.before: Abraham rose in the night, saddled his donkey, and took two young servants with him and his son Isaac. He split wood for the whole burnt offering and set out for the place God had commanded him.
changes.after: Abraham rose in the night, saddled his donkey, and took with him two young servants and his son Isaac. He split wood for the whole burnt offering and set out for the place God had commanded him.
changes.reason: Latin ‘ducens secum duos juvenes, et Isaac filium suum’; ‘took two young servants with him and his son Isaac’ can be heard aloud as ‘with him and with his son’, so the object list is kept together.

changes.before: May the young woman to whom I say, ‘Lower your jar so that I may drink,’ and who answers, ‘Drink, and I will also give your camels water,’ be the one You have prepared for Your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that You have shown kindness to my master.”
changes.after: So the young woman to whom I say, ‘Lower your jar so that I may drink,’ and who answers, ‘Drink, and I will also give your camels water’—she is the one You have prepared for Your servant Isaac. By this I shall know that You have shown kindness to my master.”
changes.reason: Latin ‘ipsa est quam præparasti’ is a statement (‘she is the one’), not a wish; the English had turned it into a prayer (‘May … be the one’).

changes.before: see, I stand beside the spring of water. May the virgin who comes out to draw water hear me say, “Give me a little water to drink from your jar,”
changes.after: see, I stand beside the spring of water. The virgin who comes out to draw water and hears me say, “Give me a little water to drink from your jar,”
changes.reason: Latin ‘virgo, quæ egredietur … audierit a me’ is the subject of the sign leading to ‘ipsa est mulier’ in 24:44, not a wish (‘May the virgin …’); restructured to match without moving content.

changes.before: and say to me, “Drink, and I will also draw for your camels.” May she be the woman the Lord has prepared for my master's son.’
changes.after: and who says to me, “Drink, and I will also draw for your camels”—she is the woman the Lord has prepared for my master's son.’
changes.reason: Latin ‘ipsa est mulier, quam præparavit Dominus’ states ‘she is the woman’, not ‘May she be the woman’; matches the Vulgate's indicative as in 24:14.

changes.before: But there too the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, “The water is ours.” Therefore, because of what happened, he named the well Dispute.
changes.after: But there too the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen, saying, “The water is ours.” Therefore, because of what happened, he named the well Calumny.
changes.reason: The Vulgate names the well ‘Calumniam’ (false accusation, Douay ‘Calumny’); ‘Dispute’ follows the Hebrew Esek rather than this column's Latin source.

changes.before: May He give you Abraham's blessings, you and your offspring after you, so that you possess the land of your sojourning, which He promised your grandfather.”
changes.after: May He give the blessings of Abraham to you and to your offspring after you, so that you possess the land of your sojourning, which He promised your grandfather.”
changes.reason: Latin ‘det tibi benedictiones Abrahæ, et semini tuo post te’: both ‘tibi’ and ‘semini tuo’ are recipients; ‘give you Abraham's blessings, you and your offspring’ trips the ear.

changes.before: When she conceived and bore a son,
changes.after: When Zilpah conceived and bore a son,
changes.reason: Latin ‘Qua’ refers back to Zilpah; after 30:9 ends on Leah's action, ‘she’ is heard as Leah, so the name is supplied (as 30:11 already supplies ‘Leah’).

changes.before: Has he not regarded us as strangers, sold us, and consumed our price?
changes.after: Has he not regarded us as strangers, sold us, and eaten up the price paid for us?
changes.reason: Latin comedit pretium nostrum means he ate up the price received for them; “consumed our price” is unclear aloud, while “eaten up the price paid for us” keeps the image and the sense.

changes.before: “I am ready,” he said to him, “Go and see whether all is well with your brothers and the animals, and report to me how things are.” Sent from the valley of Hebron, he came to Shechem.
changes.after: “I am ready,” Israel said to him, “Go and see whether all is well with your brothers and the animals, and report to me how things are.” Sent from the valley of Hebron, he came to Shechem.
changes.reason: Latin “Præsto sum, ait ei: Vade” has Joseph answer (completing 37:13’s quo respondente) and then Israel speak; with “he said to him” the card reads as if Joseph said both, so the implied subject Israel is named.

changes.before: He went in to her and said, “Allow me to lie with you,” for he did not know she was his daughter-in-law. She answered, “What will you give me to enjoy lying with me?”
changes.after: He approached her and said, “Allow me to lie with you,” for he did not know she was his daughter-in-law. She answered, “What will you give me to enjoy lying with me?”
changes.reason: Latin ingrediens ad eam ait is “approaching her, he said”; in this column “went in to her” is the idiom for intercourse (38:2, 38:8–9), which wrongly places the act before the bargaining.

changes.before: Joseph answered, “It is beyond me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
changes.after: Joseph answered, “Without me, God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
changes.reason: Absque me means “without me” (Joseph disclaims the power as his own); “It is beyond me” is heard in English as “I cannot understand it,” which the Latin does not say.

changes.before: Let him appoint overseers throughout all the regions and gather a fifth part of the produce during the seven years of fertility
changes.after: Let him appoint overseers throughout all the regions, and a fifth part of the produce during the seven years of fertility
changes.reason: The verb congreget (“let him gather”) is in 41:35, not 41:34; removing it here keeps each verse to its own Latin.

changes.before: now about to come into storehouses. Let all the grain be stored under Pharaoh's authority and kept in the cities,
changes.after: that are now about to come, let him gather into storehouses. Let all the grain be stored under Pharaoh's authority and kept in the cities,
changes.reason: Restores congreget to its own verse and fixes the misleading “now about to come into storehouses,” which made the years, not the produce, go into the storehouses.

changes.before: Israel said to them, “You have done this to my misery, telling him that you have another brother.”
changes.after: Israel said to them, “To my misery you have done this, telling him that you have another brother.”
changes.reason: In meam hoc fecistis miseriam means the deed brought misery on Jacob; “done this to my misery” is easily heard as something done to the misery itself, so the phrase is fronted.

changes.before: When they brought them, he gave them provisions for horses, sheep, oxen, and donkeys, and sustained them that year in exchange for livestock.
changes.after: When they brought them, he gave them provisions in exchange for horses, sheep, oxen, and donkeys, and sustained them that year in exchange for livestock.
changes.reason: Pro equis, et ovibus… means food given in return for the animals; “provisions for horses” is heard as fodder for the horses.

changes.before: Why should we die before your eyes? We and our land shall be yours. Buy us into the king's service and provide seed, lest the land be reduced to a wilderness when its cultivator perishes.”
changes.after: Why should we die before your eyes? We and our land shall be yours. Buy us into royal servitude and provide seed, lest the land be reduced to a wilderness when its cultivator perishes.”
changes.reason: Servitutem regiam is servitude/bondage to the king (they offer themselves as the king's servi), which “the king's service” softens into employment.

changes.before: Binding his colt to the vine, and his female donkey to the vine, O my son, he shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape.
changes.after: Binding his colt to the vineyard, and his female donkey to the vine, O my son, he shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape.
changes.reason: The Latin pairs two different words, ad vineam (to the vineyard) and ad vitem (to the vine); the current reading says “vine” twice and loses the parallel.
